statement: Denmark secured permanent exemptions from provisions of the Maastricht Treaty (1993), notably regarding participation in Economic and Monetary Union (the euro) and in security and defence policy, following the Edinburgh Decision of the European Council in December 1992. These are permanent derogations from primary EU law, not transitional periods. Denmark itself later decided, by referendum following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, to participate in the defence and security policy; the EMU exemption remained in force.
statement_is: Danmörk tryggði sér árið 1992 varanlegar undanþágur frá Maastricht-sáttmálanum á grundvelli Edinburgh-ákvörðunar Evrópuráðsins, einkum varðandi þátttöku í Efnahags- og myntbandalaginu (evrusvæðið) og utanríkis- og varnarmálastefnu. Þær eru varanleg frávik frá meginmálalögum ESB; Danmörk afturkallaði varnarundanþáguna með þjóðaratkvæðagreiðslu árið 2022 í kjölfar innrásar Rússlands í Úkraínu, en undanþágan frá evrusvæðinu er enn í gildi.
source_name: Evrópuvefurinn — Margrét Einarsdóttir, „Er eitthvað um að semja þegar ríki gera aðildarsamning við ESB?" (prófessor við lagadeild HR / Reykjavík University, 2026)
source_description_is: Evrópuvefurinn er íslenskur fræðsluvefur um ESB-málefni þar sem sérfræðingar svara spurningum almennings; Margrét Einarsdóttir er prófessor við lagadeild Háskólans í Reykjavík.
caveats: Primary source cited in the answer: the Edinburgh European Council Decision, December 1992, later confirmed in the Lisbon Treaty (the answer does not cite specific protocol numbers; Denmark's opt-outs are in Protocol No. 22 to the Lisbon Treaty, with the Schengen position in Protocol No. 19). The answer states Denmark reversed the defence opt-out by popular vote after Russia's invasion of Ukraine but does not give the referendum date (it was 1 June 2022); the EMU exemption was not part of that vote.
